clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Bacterial Meningitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Bacterial Meningitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Acute bacterial meningitis is a true medical emergency: empiric IV antibiotics and dexamethasone must be started within 60 minutes of suspicion and should never be delayed for neuroimaging or lumbar puncture.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: high fever 39.5C, severe headache, neck stiffness, and light sensitivity

Key HPI features: 34F brought by family due to rapid onset of high fever, excruciating headache, stiff neck, and extreme sensitivity to light (photophobia) over the past 12 hours. Appears drowsy and slow to answer.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 39.6C, HR 118, BP 100/62, RR 20. Nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs. GCS 13 (drowsy, oriented x2). Photophobia limiting exam. No petechial rash.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Bacterial Meningitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Viral meningitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Drowsiness or slow responses — rapid deterioration.
management_principles: Immediately draw blood cultures, then start empiric IV Ceftriaxone, Vancomycin, and Dexamethasone without delay.
Assess for signs of raised intracranial pressure or focal neurologic deficit to decide whether head CT is needed before lumbar puncture.
Perform lumbar puncture as soon as safely possible for CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, gram stain, culture).
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 34F brought in by family with rapid-onset (12 hours) high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia; appears drowsy and slow to answer.
reference_soap.objective: T 39.6C, HR 118, BP 100/62, RR 20. Nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs. GCS 13 (drowsy, oriented x2). No petechial rash.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Bacterial Meningitis — medical emergency requiring immediate empiric antibiotics.
reference_soap.plan: Treat as a medical emergency: obtain blood cultures immediately, then administer IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and dexamethasone without delaying for imaging or lumbar puncture. Because drowsiness may indicate increased intracranial-pressure risk, obtain head CT before LP when clinically indicated, but do not allow CT to delay antimicrobials. Perform LP promptly once safe and involve critical care/Infectious Diseases.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Acute Bacterial Meningitis, medical emergency.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for high fever 39.5C, severe headache, neck stiffness, and light sensitivity
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for infectious disease
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Acute Bacterial Meningitis, medical emergency.

teaching.one_liner: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection of the meninges causing fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia with declining alertness — treat with antibiotics and steroids immediately, imaging should not delay treatment.
red_flags: Drowsiness or slow responses — rapid deterioration

must_ask.say: How quickly did this come on — over hours?
Does moving your neck hurt, and is light bothering you?
Has she been slow to answer or seem drowsy?
How high has the fever gone?
Has she been around anyone sick recently, or had a recent infection?

history.answer: My head is throbbing agonizingly, and I am burning up with a terrible high fever. Moving my neck hurts terribly, and the room light is blinding me.
It came on suddenly about 12 hours ago, late last night, and worsened very rapidly.
My temperature reached 39.5 degrees Celsius on the home thermometer, and I have been shaking with severe chills.
My family gave me some acetaminophen about four hours ago, but the fever and headache did not improve at all.
No, I do not have any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or shortness of breath.
No, I have no pain or burning when I urinate, no frequent urination, and no flank pain.
I felt very nauseated and threw up once from the headache, but I have no abdominal pain or diarrhea.
It is the most excruciating headache I have ever felt all over my head, and my neck feels completely stiff and locked.
Yes, even normal indoor lighting feels intensely painful to look at, so I have to keep my eyes shut.
I feel exhausted, heavy, and very drowsy. It takes a lot of effort for me to think and speak.
No, I haven't seen any rash, purple spots, black scabs from bug bites, or swollen joints.
No, this illness started acutely last night, so there has been no night sweats or weight loss.
No, I haven't felt any swollen lumps in my neck, underarms, or groin.
No, I have not traveled outside the city, haven't gone hiking or done farm work, and haven't handled any animals.
No one in my home or office has been sick with high fever or headaches.
I had a mild stuffy nose about a week ago that seemed to clear up, but nothing severe.
No, I have never had cancer treatment, and I am not taking steroids or immunosuppressive drugs.
No, I have never had a heart murmur or artificial heart valve, and I have not had any dental work recently.
No, I have not started any new prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements.
I have one long-term partner, and I have never used intravenous drugs or shared needles.
I have always been healthy with no chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or health supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I drink an occasional glass of beer with friends once or twice a month, but nothing recently.
I work an office desk job in administration, and I live in an apartment with my family.
There is no family history of meningitis, neurological conditions, or premature cardiovascular disease.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago and was normal, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.
My family is terrified that I have meningitis or bleeding inside my brain, and I am scared of permanent brain damage or dying.
We want an emergency spinal tap and whatever intravenous antibiotics are necessary right away.

exam.finding: Temperature 39.6 C, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Acutely ill-appearing female lying still with eyes closed, clearly photophobic, drowsy, and responding slowly.
Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13; drowsy and oriented to person and place but disoriented to time, answering questions with delayed latency.
Marked nuchal rigidity is present, with positive Kernig sign and positive Brudzinski sign.
Bilateral tympanic membranes are translucent and pearly gray without erythema, bulging, or middle ear fluid.
Posterior pharynx is clear without erythema, exudates, or tonsillar swelling.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without crackles, wheezing, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender to light and deep palpation without guarding or rigidity.
No tenderness upon percussion over either costovertebral angle.
Skin is warm and flushed without petechiae, purpura, maculopapular rash, or eschar.
